summary: A 1977 description of the SUPDUP protocol, a remote terminal protocol developed at MIT that supports display terminals better than plain Telnet. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: SUPDUP is a remote terminal protocol designed for display terminals. It lets a server request operations such as moving the cursor or clearing part of a screen while allowing simpler terminals to use fewer features.

questions: how did supdup describe terminal capabilities
what display operations could supdup send
subtitle: A device-independent remote display protocol that supports cursor and screen operations.

tldr.problem: Telnet does not use the full display capabilities of terminals, and individual terminal protocols are device-specific.
tldr.mechanism: SUPDUP defines virtual display operations and sends terminal capabilities to the server so it can use supported cursor, erase and insert/delete functions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes an operational protocol used between MIT ITS systems and some other display environments at the time of writing; the unit metadata marks it Historic.

today: RFC 734 is Historic according to the unit metadata. It documents SUPDUP's display protocol and describes the systems and terminal environments known to the author in 1977.

sections.title: A Virtual Display Terminal
sections.content:
RFC 734 describes SUPDUP as a highly efficient display Telnet protocol. It began as a private protocol between MIT ITS systems and was also used with some display terminals at other sites.

SUPDUP defines a virtual terminal using operations common to display terminals rather than one terminal's own protocol. It can also support terminals that lack some display functions, down to a Teletype Model 33. Unlike Telnet, SUPDUP takes advantage of display-terminal capabilities and operates independently from Telnet.
sections.plainLanguage: SUPDUP gives remote systems a shared set of display commands. A terminal can use the commands it supports and still connect if it lacks some display features.

sections.title: Initialization and Terminal Capabilities
sections.content:
The SUPDUP server listens on octal socket 137. After the Initial Connection Protocol completes, the user sends terminal settings as 36-bit words, each carried in six 6-bit bytes. The first word gives the negative count of variables that follow.

The settings include terminal type, options, screen height, line width and scrolling behavior. The server responds with an ASCII greeting ending in %TDNOP, after which the parties exchange terminal input and display codes. The terminal type must be 7 (%TNSFW).
sections.plainLanguage: When connecting, the user's program tells the server what the terminal can do and how large its screen is. The server then sends its greeting and display output.

sections.title: Input and Display Operations
sections.content:
Input can use standard 7-bit ASCII or a 12-bit extended character set with modifier bits, including CONTROL and META. The protocol uses octal 034 as an escape for commands; a literal 034 is sent twice. Characters with modifier bits use a three-byte sequence beginning with 034.

On output, codes below octal 200 are printing characters. Codes at or above 200 are %TD display operations. Examples include %TDMOV to move the cursor, %TDEOL to erase to the end of a line, %TDCLR to clear the screen, and codes to insert or delete lines and characters. Unknown %TD codes should be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: SUPDUP sends ordinary characters directly and uses special codes for screen actions. The special codes can move the cursor, erase text or insert and delete lines and characters.

sections.title: Reset Handling and Terminal Options
sections.content:
The user's terminal options report supported features, such as selective erase, cursor movement, scrolling, insert/delete operations and extended characters. A terminal that cannot perform an operation can indicate that limitation in its options.

When a network interrupt disrupts output, the server suspends output until the user reports the current cursor position. The user program should stop or abort output when possible and respond to the server's output-reset code with the current screen position.
sections.plainLanguage: The user reports which display features are available. After an output reset, it reports the cursor position so the server can continue from a known location.
